samples.text:
People today have many choices about how to spend their money. Some people believe it is better to spend money on experiences like travelling and concerts, while others think buying things that last for a long time is wiser. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, spending money on experiences has many advantages. When people travel to other countries, they can learn about different cultures, try new food and meet new people. These memories stays with them for their whole life. For example, most of people still remember a family holiday from their childhood, but they have forgotten the toys they had. Also, sharing experiences with friends and family can make the relationship stronger.

On the other hand, buying possessions also has benefits. Things like a house, a car or good furniture can be used for many years and make daily life more comfortable. Some possessions, such as property or gold, can even increase in value, so they are a kind of investment for the future. In contrast, a holiday finishes after one or two weeks and the money is gone. For people who do not have much money, it is more sensible to buy useful things than spending on expensive trips.

In my opinion, experiences are more valuable than possessions, as long as people do not waste money they need for basic things. After buying the necessary items, people should spend their extra money for experiences which make them happy and help them learn.

In conclusion, both experiences and possessions have advantages. I believe experiences give more happiness in the long term, but people should first make sure they have what they need in their daily life.
samples.why: Addresses both views and gives a clear opinion · relevant examples but ideas stay general · simple linking (Also, In contrast) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, quantifier and preposition errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
How people choose to spend their disposable income reflects their priorities in life. Some believe that experiences such as travel, concerts and meals out offer the best value, while others argue that it is more sensible to invest in lasting possessions. In my view, experiences generally bring greater long-term satisfaction, although certain durable goods are clearly worthwhile.

Those who favour possessions emphasise their practical and financial value. Items such as a reliable car, quality furniture or a home can be used every day for many years, improving comfort and convenience long after the purchase. Some possessions, particularly property, may even increase in value and provide financial security in the future. By comparison, the money spent on a weekend away or an expensive concert is gone within days, leaving nothing tangible behind.

On the other hand, supporters of experiences argue that their benefits last longer than they first appear. Memories of travelling to a new country, learning a skill or celebrating with friends can bring pleasure for decades, and they often become part of a person's identity. Material goods, by contrast, tend to lose their appeal quickly as people become used to them or replace them with newer model. Experiences are also frequently shared, which strengthens relationships, whereas possessions can encourage comparison and competition with others.

In my opinion, the wisest approach is to buy durable items that genuinely improve daily life, and then to prioritise experiences with any remaining money. Spending on unnecessary luxury goods, which quickly become old-fashioned, is less rewarding than investing in activities that broaden one's horizons.

In conclusion, while lasting possessions provide comfort and security, I believe experiences such as travel and entertainment usually offer more lasting happiness, and they deserve a significant share of people's spending.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended and supported · logical progression with clear topic sentences · good collocations (disposable income, broaden one's horizons) · frequent error-free sentences with one article slip.

samples.text:
Decisions about how to spend money reveal much about what people value. Some argue that the wisest use of income is to pay for experiences, such as travel and entertainment, whereas others maintain that it is more prudent to buy possessions that will last. While both have a place in a balanced life, I believe that experiences generally offer the greater and more enduring reward, once essential needs have been met.

The case for durable possessions is grounded in practicality. A well-made coat, a dependable vehicle or a comfortable home provides tangible benefits every day, often for many years, and the cost per use of a quality item can be remarkably low. Certain assets, notably property, may also appreciate in value, offering a degree of financial security that no holiday can match. From this perspective, spending heavily on fleeting experiences might seem short-sighted, particularly for those on modest incomes.

Nevertheless, the value of experiences is frequently underestimated. Although a journey or a concert is over quickly, the memories it creates can be revisited for a lifetime and often grow more cherished with time. Experiences also tend to be shared, strengthening bonds with family and friends, and they can broaden perspectives in ways that possessions rarely do, whether through exposure to another culture or the acquisition of a new skill. By contrast, the pleasure derived from a new purchase often fades as people grow accustomed to it, prompting a cycle of further buying that brings diminishing satisfaction.

In my view, therefore, the most sensible approach is to invest in a limited number of durable, genuinely useful items and to devote discretionary spending largely to experiences. This avoids accumulating possessions that bring little lasting joy, while still providing the stability that essential goods offer.

In conclusion, although possessions that last can deliver comfort and security, experiences tend to provide richer and longer-lasting fulfilment, and they therefore represent the wiser use of money beyond life's necessities.
samples.why: Both views fully developed with thoughtful support · clear, qualified opinion · logical sequencing and well-managed paragraphs · wide, precise vocabulary (appreciate in value, discretionary spending) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
